items.t: Czech Protesters Rally Against Plan to Scrap Broadcasting Fees
items.s: Organizers said between 350,000 and 450,000 people joined a protest in Prague against the government’s plan to abolish broadcasting fees. The plan would finance public broadcasters from the state budget instead.
p: Organizers said between 350,000 and 450,000 people took part in a protest in Prague against the government’s plan to abolish broadcasting fees in Czechia. Many travelled from other cities by bus and train, leaving public transport overcrowded.

Protesters argue the plan could place public broadcasters under the control of the right-wing government led by Prime Minister Andrej Babis. Babis defended the proposal last week, saying his government is not interested in controlling or nationalizing public media, and called the protesters’ claims untrue. Foreign Minister Petr Macinka accused the organizers of turning demonstrations into a business model.

Under the plan, public broadcasters would be funded from the state budget rather than through fees. The government argues that editorial independence will not be affected and that broadcasters need to cut costs. The suggested reform would reduce public media’s budget by 15 percent, and critics say the government wants more influence over the outlets.

Since the plan was introduced in April, several large protests have taken place, and Czech TV and radio held a one-day strike against it. The European Broadcasting Union, the European Federation of Journalists and Reporters Without Borders have all criticized the proposal.

The governing coalition consists of Babis’s ANO party, the far-right SPD and the Eurosceptic Motorists. Polls show ANO still has around 30 percent support, even as the protests targeted the coalition. According to the Reuters Institute Digital News Report 2026, trust in media in Czechia is low, at 30 to 33 percent, though public broadcasters are still regarded as “the most trusted brands.”
items.cav: The protester and organizer figures are unverified claims, and the sources do not give an independent count. The claim that the government seeks control of public media is the view of critics and protesters, while the government denies it.
items.op: Funding public broadcasters from the state budget may be defensible on cost grounds, but it hands ministers a lever over the newsroom. Before any cut takes effect, the government should show in public how editorial independence will be protected.

items.t: Spain and England meet in Madrid with top spot in Nations League Group A at stake
items.s: England and Spain meet in Madrid in the final group game of the UEFA Nations League, with both sides already through to the quarter-finals. The Guardian’s live coverage gives the lineups and Thomas Tuchel’s pre-match comments.
p: The match is scheduled to kick off at 7.45pm GMT in Madrid. Both teams have already qualified for the last eight, so the contest is about who finishes first in the group. According to the Guardian’s live blog, the group winner will face an unseeded side in the quarter-finals, with the second leg played at home. The competition resumes at the end of March.

Tuchel told ITV that “it’s a beautiful match”, and the Guardian’s preview argues that England have a good chance because of how Spain have set up. Spain are without Rodri, and Pedri is not in the squad, with Mikel Merino coming in for Fermín López. Lamine Yamal returns after being rested for the 2-0 win away to Czechia, and Oyarzabal starts as the centre-forward.

Spain are set to line up in a 4-3-3 with Unai Simon in goal, Marc Pubill, Cubarsi, Aymeric Laporte and Cucurella in defence, and Zubimendi, Fabián Ruiz and Merino in midfield. Pedro Porro, important at the World Cup, drops out. England pick a 4-2-3-1 with Jordan Pickford replaced by Trafford in goal, and a Konsa and Quansah centre-back pairing. Dan Burn is left out, Ben White starts at right-back, and Lewis Hall plays at left-back. Declan Rice and Elliot Anderson form the double pivot, with Kane leading the line.

The Guardian’s preview points to Kane dropping deep and Gordon and Rogers attacking the space behind Spain’s high line. The writer expects Spain to try to pull England’s midfielders wide, which the England side must avoid doing. The preview also says Spain’s defence was exposed at Wembley, where Spain won 3-2 and Harry Kane missed a penalty that would have made it 3-1 to England.

The fixture comes after England’s defeat in the World Cup semi-final, which the Guardian’s writer describes as a painful failure. That loss, and England’s earlier defeat in the Euro final, are used as reasons to ask whether the team can impose its own game rather than wait for the match to end.

Al Jazeera also has a live page for the fixture, but the material available to us for that outlet consists only of a summary and team-news headline, so its account of the match adds little beyond confirming the fixture and its status as the final group game.
items.cav: Most of the detail comes from a Guardian live-blog preview that mixes reporting with the writer’s opinion, so the tactical predictions are the author’s expectations, not confirmed plans. The Al Jazeera pages offered only short summaries, and no final score or result is available in these sources.
items.op: England’s tournament record should not be reduced to a single result, but the pattern the Guardian describes deserves scrutiny. Tuchel’s side must show it can play its own game rather than retreat, and the accountability for that choice belongs in public view.

items.t: Estonia to close all Russian border crossings after foiled drone factory arson plot
items.s: Estonia says it foiled an attempted Russian arson attack on a drone factory and will shut every border crossing with Russia by December 1. Prime Minister Karsten Michal blamed Russia’s GRU intelligence service.
p: Estonian authorities said on Sunday that they had stopped an attempted arson attack on a drone factory run by the defence company Threod Systems in Viimsi. Prime Minister Karsten Michal said the GRU, Russia’s military intelligence service, was behind the attempt, which he said took place on Saturday night.

Michal said “extensive damage” had been averted after law enforcement responded and detained the suspected attackers. He described the episode as part of a wider Russian hybrid war against Europe, aimed at reducing support for Ukraine.

Hours later, Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said Estonia would close all border crossings with Russia by December 1. He wrote on social media that hostile actions would not go unanswered and that the closure would limit Russia’s ability to carry out hostile activity and help prevent sanctions circumvention.

Tsahkna said he had informed the foreign ministers of Finland, Latvia and Lithuania. Estonia has several crossings with Russia and had until now been one of the few European Union states to keep them open.

The sources do not give details of the suspects’ identities, any charges, or the evidence linking the GRU to the plot. The attribution comes from the Estonian government and has not been independently confirmed.
items.cav: The Russian link is the Estonian government’s claim and is not independently verified. Reports differ on whether the factory was set alight or the arson was foiled, and the sources give no detail on the suspects.
items.op: Closing a border is a blunt instrument, and it lands on ordinary travellers and businesses who had nothing to do with the plot. If Tallinn wants the public to accept such costs, it should publish the evidence tying the GRU to the attack. Security measures need the same transparency as the threat they answer.

items.t: Canary Islands take roughly 1,500 arrivals in a single day, with El Hierro absorbing most of them
items.s: Roughly 1,500 to 1,600 people reached Spain’s Canary Islands on Saturday, most of them at El Hierro, according to figures reported by different outlets. The surge follows a larger crisis in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta.
p: Spanish news agency EFE reported on Sunday, using tallies from the Spanish government’s maritime rescue body, that 1,580 people had arrived on Saturday. Most of them were brought to El Hierro, the smallest of the main islands in the archipelago’s western group, in 15 open wooden vessels. DW put the total for Friday and Saturday combined at more than 2,300.

Al Jazeera cited the Spanish rescue service with a lower figure for Saturday: 1,488 people taken from 14 dinghies, known as pirogues. It said that daily total exceeded a previous record of 1,461 set in November 2020. Al Jazeera also reported that more than 9,000 people have arrived in the territory since the start of November, and that Spain has declared a migration emergency there.

Most of those arriving departed from West African coasts, including Senegal, Gambia and Guinea. DW said the largest share came from those countries. Al Jazeera reported that one boat on Saturday carried 240 people, among them 12 women and 36 children, and that the International Organization for Migration had recorded at least 450 deaths on the Western African Atlantic route in the first ten months of the year.

Spain’s Territorial Policy Minister, Angel Victor Torres Perez, visited La Restinga, a town at the southern tip of El Hierro, on Sunday. She thanked residents for their solidarity and commitment. In a post on X, she said the government intends to handle the surge with humanity and with the island’s residents in mind. El Hierro has a population of nearly 12,000.

DW noted that overall migration to the islands fell 5.5 per cent between January and October 31 compared with the same period last year, so the recent spike is a sharp reversal within a broader decline. The surge also follows the events in late July, when an estimated 80,000 people, mostly young Moroccan men, crossed from Morocco into Ceuta. Al Jazeera reported that at least 100 people died during that crossing and that Spain deported more than a dozen of those who entered.

Al Jazeera said the European Union’s new Pact on Migration and Asylum took effect on June 12, 2026, and that the new rules have not stopped the flow of migrants to Spain. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has faced opposition criticism over his handling of Ceuta, and migration and housing are expected to be major issues for voters ahead of snap elections later this month.
items.cav: The sources give different figures for Saturday’s arrivals (1,580 in EFE’s tally as reported by DW, 1,488 in the rescue service figures reported by Al Jazeera) and do not explain the gap. The “more than 9,000” total and the record claim come from Al Jazeera alone, and the record’s comparison period is not detailed beyond the 2020 figure.
items.op: Numbers this large are easily reduced to statistics, yet each boat carries people who face real risk at sea. Spain’s government should publish consistent arrival and rescue counts, and explain its reception and deportation procedures in public. Emergency measures that lack transparency erode the public trust they depend on.

items.t: Estonia to close all Russian border crossings after alleged GRU-ordered attack on drone maker
items.s: Estonia will shut all its border crossings with Russia from 1 December, its foreign minister said, after eight people were detained over an attempted attack on a defence company that Tallinn blames on Russian military intelligence. The Kremlin has not commented on this case.
p: The Estonian government says Russia’s GRU military intelligence service ordered an attempted attack on Threod Systems, a Tallinn-area defence company that makes long-range attack and reconnaissance drones. Authorities said the aim was to cause an explosion and set the building on fire. The attack was reported to have taken place on Saturday, with eight people detained. No injuries or damage were reported by the company’s security team, though the prime minister said wider damage had been averted thanks to heightened security and a fast police response.

Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna announced on Sunday, on X, that all Estonian-Russian border crossing points would close from 1 December. He cited what he called “clear evidence” of the GRU’s role, although the sources do not show that evidence. Estonia has three open crossings with Russia, at Narva, Koidula and Luhamaa. Authorities have not said how long the closure will last.

Prime Minister Kristen Michal said the closure was meant to reduce the risk of further attacks and to signal that assaults on the country’s defence industry would not be tolerated. He tied the incidents to Estonia’s support for Ukraine, arguing that Moscow wants Tallinn to become fearful and to weaken that backing. The government says it will tighten security and work more closely with businesses and allies.

Chief prosecutor Astrid Asi told reporters that the eight suspects live in Latvia. Al Jazeera, citing Latvian officials, described the arrests as involving “Latvian citizens and non-citizens”, which is a slightly different description. Estonia’s internal security service, Kapo, has asked a court to keep five of those detained in custody. The suspects have not been tried, and their guilt has not been established.

This is the second attempted attack on an Estonian defence firm that authorities have linked to Russia. An arson attack at Milrem Robotics in August was described by Kapo in September as a deliberate, pre-planned operation carried out for Russian special services. At that time Estonia summoned Russia’s chargé d’affaires, and the Kremlin rejected the accusation as baseless. Moscow has not yet responded publicly to the latest claims.

European intelligence agencies have warned for some time about sabotage against defence firms and Russian efforts to recruit people online for such acts. Mihkelson, chairman of the Estonian parliament’s foreign affairs committee, said the arrests showed the country could respond quickly, but argued that diplomatic protests alone were not enough.
items.cav: The sources do not publish the evidence behind the GRU attribution, and the Kremlin’s response to this specific incident is not yet known. Accounts differ on the timing (Saturday morning or night) and on the detainees’ nationality, and the damage reports vary between outlets.
items.op: Blaming Moscow may be justified, but closing every crossing is a blunt tool that also hits ordinary travellers and trade. Estonia should publish the evidence behind its attribution so that a measure this sweeping rests on proof the public can examine.

items.t: Hundreds of thousands rally in Prague against plan to fund Czech public media from the state budget
items.s: Organisers said more than 350,000 people joined a Sunday rally in Prague against a government plan to scrap licence fees for public broadcasters. Critics say the change would give ministers more influence over newsrooms.
p: Hundreds of thousands of Czechs gathered in Prague on Sunday to protest against a plan by Prime Minister Andrej Babiš’s government to end the mandatory licence fees that fund Czech Television and Czech Radio. Organisers said more than 350,000 people attended, which they described as one of the largest demonstrations in the country’s history. Euronews, citing media reports, put the figure at 350,000 to 400,000.

The rally was held at Letná Plain, the site of the 1989 Velvet Revolution that ended more than four decades of communist rule. Many participants wore triangular paper hats resembling Večerníček, an animated bedtime-story character who has become a symbol of the movement. Banners included the slogan “We won’t give media away.”

The government wants to finance the two broadcasters from the state budget instead. Protesters argue this would give ministers more leverage over editorial decisions. Sources say the future state subsidy would be far below current licence-fee revenue. The proposed changes would cut state television and radio budgets by about 15 per cent, according to the Guardian.

The organising group, Million Moments for Democracy, said the authorities would now see the scale of opposition. Its lead organiser, Mikuláš Minář, said the event was “just a beginning.” In a statement, the group demanded that the government withdraw the plan and accused Babiš and his partners of treating democratic institutions as their own property.

Euronews reported that the protest was tied to a vote in the Chamber of Deputies on the amendment, which the group summarised with the slogan “Never again 4:36”. According to Euronews, the majority cut short the debate, leaving more than 60 opposition MPs unable to speak. The Guardian dates the first reading to late October, and Euronews to mid-October, so the sources differ on timing.

The European Broadcasting Union, the European Federation of Journalists, Reporters Without Borders and the International Press Institute have criticised the plan. They compared it with moves in Slovakia and Hungary, where media independence has been weakened under populist governments.

Babiš, a billionaire who returned to power last year, said the protests were based on unfounded claims. In an opinion piece he wrote that the government would not interfere in editorial work. Euronews also reported that students, theatres, writers, athletes, churches and healthcare workers voiced support for public media. Police said the demonstration passed without incident until early evening.
items.cav: Crowd estimates differ: the Guardian cites organisers’ figure of more than 350,000, while Euronews reports 350,000 to 400,000 from media reports. The timing of the first parliamentary reading is also reported differently. The 15 per cent budget cut and the fee amounts come from the sources and were not independently verified.
items.op: Public broadcasters need funding that cannot be turned into a lever over what they report. Moving them onto the state budget, while the government controls the purse, invites exactly that pressure. Parliament should answer the protesters with open debate and a full hearing, not a rushed vote in the small hours.

items.t: Iran launches second drone attack on US base in Bahrain in three days
items.s: Iranian drones were aimed at a US military base in Bahrain on Sunday, according to the Guardian and the BBC, in the second such attempt in three days. The strikes further undermine stalled efforts to end the wider conflict.
p: Blasts were heard over Bahrain on Sunday after Iranian drones were aimed at a US base on the island kingdom, according to the Guardian. It was the second such attack in three days, and Tehran framed it as retaliation for recent US strikes inside Iran. The Guardian also said the episode deepened fears of escalation just as talks between Tehran and Washington appear stuck.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps said it sent six drones toward a US air defence radar at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base, which the BBC spells al-Riffa. The IRGC described the move as a response to “hostile US actions”. Bahraini authorities said their air defences stopped the drones before they reached their targets, and the BBC reported that the country’s military said the drones were destroyed before they could achieve their aims.

One report said Bahrain issued two alerts about possible threats on Sunday, its first such warnings since September, as explosions rattled the capital, Manama. Sirens were heard across the country, and the interior ministry told residents to move to the nearest secure place.

Bahrain’s foreign ministry denounced the attacks as brutal and said it holds Iran entirely accountable for what follows. Jordan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Qatar also condemned the strikes and voiced support for Bahrain.

The latest attack followed an earlier one on Friday. The IRGC said it had hit a US early warning radar, but the US military denied that and said it had shot down two one-way drones with no injuries or damage. Before that, US forces struck Iranian targets, including Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz. US officials told CBS the strikes were limited and defensive, and were a response to Iranian fire at a US aircraft. Iran’s state news agency Irna reported explosions on the island.

Diplomacy looks stalled. The conflict began in February with joint US and Israeli attacks on Iran, and a preliminary agreement reached in June fell apart within weeks. According to the Guardian, Donald Trump has said Washington is no longer seeking a deal and has asked Vice-President JD Vance to focus on alleged corruption and fraud in Democrat-run cities and states. Vance had requested a personal meeting with Iranian negotiators. Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmaeil Baghaei, said Tehran was “not waiting for anyone”.

In the Strait of Hormuz, the IRGC claimed that two ships struck mines and that one oil supertanker carrying 2m barrels sank. There has been no immediate independent confirmation of that claim. The US military has said it cleared all mines from the main routes through the waterway.

In Yemen, Iran-aligned Houthi rebels pushed forward against pro-government forces in the south. The main government-backed force announced it was pulling back from the Bab el-Mandeb area to defend Aden. AFP, citing military and government sources, reported that a Houthi missile strike near Aden killed people and wounded 12.
items.cav: The IRGC’s claims about the drone attacks and the tanker sinking have not been independently verified, and the US military disputes some of them. The casualty figures in Yemen are second-hand, relayed by AFP from unnamed sources.
items.op: Drone strikes on a host nation and threats to shipping leave little room for deals made behind closed doors. Whoever is responsible for each attack, the public deserves verified accounts of what was fired, where and why. A policy that shifts from negotiation to retaliation without explanation is the costliest route for everyone in the Gulf.

items.t: Thousands rally in Prague against plan to fund Czech public media from state budget
items.s: Thousands of people gathered in central Prague on Sunday to oppose the Czech government's plan to end the licence fee and pay for public media from the state budget. The government says editorial independence will be preserved.
p: Demonstrators argue that the proposal could give politicians room to limit media freedom. The ruling coalition, made up of the populist ANO party and two right-wing Eurosceptic parties, counters that broadcasters must reduce their spending and that editorial decisions would remain unaffected.

Parliament approved the first reading of the bill late last month, and protests have continued since then. At present, Czech households pay 205 crowns ($9.44; £7.06) per month for television and radio services.

The Million Moments for Democracy association, which organised Sunday's march, put attendance at “roughly 400,000.” That number comes from the organisers, and the reporting does not include an independent count.

Milana Rudolfova, a 72-year-old pensioner, told Reuters that she regards Czech Television as a reliable source of truth. Some marchers wore paper hats folded from newspaper in honour of Vecernicek, the cartoon figure who has long presented the broadcaster's evening children's stories.

Prime Minister Andrej Babis, who was appointed in December 2025, has rejected the idea that his government wants to control public media. Speaking to the Czech News Agency, he argued that the current system is outdated and that many European countries are adopting similar models.

Several European states have already left the licence fee behind. France abolished it in 2022, and its public broadcasters are now financed partly through a share of VAT revenue. Norway ended its fee in 2020 and placed public broadcasting costs within the national budget.

Critics have drawn parallels with Hungary under former Prime Minister Viktor Orban, who exercised tight control over state media during his time in office. In June, Pavol Szalai of Reporters Without Borders said that attacks on both private and public outlets had become a defining feature of Babis's tenure.
items.cav: The attendance figure is the organisers' own estimate, and the Hungary comparison is made by unnamed critics. The sources do not explain how the new funding model would operate in practice.
items.op: Public broadcasting should not depend on a government's promises about how it will behave. If the Czech state takes over its funding, the law must set firm safeguards for editorial independence and make the terms of any budget decision public. Assurances from the prime minister are not enough.

items.t: Duffy blames prior presidents and Congress for nationwide flight stoppage; Van Hollen says funds were underused
items.s: The US transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, blamed earlier administrations and a lack of congressional funding for the travel chaos after a four-hour nationwide flight stoppage. A Democratic senator argued the Trump administration has not properly spent money it already received.
p: Donald Trump’s administration on Sunday attributed the travel disruption that followed Friday’s four-hour nationwide flight stoppage to prior presidents and to insufficient congressional funding, according to The Guardian. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop led to the delay or cancellation of thousands of flights.

Speaking to CNN, Duffy said: “I take responsibility for what was given to me.” He had earlier said that routine but necessary maintenance, botched by a contractor, caused the stoppage. He argued that the $12.5bn Congress provided was limited in scope and not nearly enough. He said it could not pay for new telecom architecture, new air traffic software or new towers, and that the existing systems date back to the 1990s.

Democratic senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland rejected that argument. He told CNN that it was “really rich” for the secretary to blame Congress, which he said had given the administration what it requested. In his view, the administration has not properly invested all the funds already allocated for upgrades. He said that if more money is needed, the administration should come forward and justify it.

Trump, who waited until Sunday to comment on the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years, blamed the Biden administration in a Truth Social post. He wrote that the administration had “the knowledge and plan” for flight control systems and that Congress needed to provide the money. Duffy said Trump had been in constant behind-the-scenes contact and was fully tracking events, though the report does not independently confirm this.

On CBS News’ Face the Nation, Duffy said the FAA was investigating the root cause of the botched work, which involved replacing old copper telecommunication lines with fiber optic cables. He said similar work had been done “thousands of times” without problems. The contractor, L3Harris, is reportedly conducting diagnostic tests. Duffy repeated that there was no sign of a foreign cyberattack.

The union Professional Aviation Safety Specialists (Pass), which represents more than 11,000 FAA workers, said its technicians were not involved in the upgrades behind the stoppage. It said the issue was isolated to two contractor-owned and contractor-maintained routers, and that contractors have historically followed a protocol in which FAA employees conduct a risk assessment. Asked whether a risk assessment was carried out in this case, Duffy did not directly answer, saying only: “We do risk assessments on everything.”

Duffy also cited a Government Accountability Office report from September 2026 that called for modernizing air traffic control systems, and he rejected concerns that speed was being prioritised over cost and disruption. Pass has called for better staffing of certified technicians and for a fuller role for its members in the modernisation effort.
items.cav: The accounts conflict: Duffy says the work was done appropriately, while the union says its technicians were not involved and questions the usual risk-assessment protocol. The root cause is still under investigation, and the contractor’s diagnostics are only reportedly under way. Trump’s claimed involvement is based on Duffy’s account and is not independently confirmed.
items.op: Whoever is at fault, the public is entitled to a clear account of who approved the work, what risk checks were done, and how the funds were spent. Blame passed between administrations and Congress does not answer those questions. Transparency about the investigation should come before any further political argument.

items.t: Gulf states condemn Iranian drone attack on Bahrain as Hormuz tensions rise
items.s: Jordan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Qatar have condemned an Iranian attack on Bahrain, which Bahraini authorities said was intercepted. The strike is the latest sign that a two-month lull in fighting may be ending.
p: Early on Sunday, Iran reportedly sent six drones toward a US air base in Bahrain, raising fears that full-scale fighting could resume. Bahraini authorities said they had stopped the incoming threat and destroyed the drones before impact, and gave no immediate account of any harm to property or people.

The island state, which is home to a major US naval command, issued public warnings and activated missile sirens before the strikes arrived. Residents, who were hit by the second attack since Friday, said they were unsettled to see the violence return. One local resident voiced hope that the earlier calm would hold.

Tehran said its target was a radar installation at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base and described the operation as a response to recent American military action. Washington had not yet commented on the Sunday attack, though it has previously said the first attempt on Friday caused no damage.

The Bahraini state news agency published reactions from several governments in the region. Saudi Arabia’s Foreign Ministry called the Iranian strikes a breach of international law and of the duty of good neighbourly conduct, urging an end to them. Qatar’s Foreign Ministry cautioned that the attacks marked a hazardous escalation that could derail diplomacy aimed at calming the region.

The incident sits within a broader standoff. US forces have conducted limited strikes on Iranian naval positions along the southern coast and on Qeshm Island, in the Strait of Hormuz, with the stated aim of protecting oil tankers using the waterway. Iran insists that vessels crossing the strait without its approval are striking mines and sinking, and says it regards them as lawful targets.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guards asserted that a supertanker loaded with more than two million barrels of oil had sunk after hitting a mine in the strait, and that two other ships had struck its mines. No independent confirmation of the tanker claim is available. Earlier, the US military had said it had cleared mines from the main shipping lanes.

Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei told a news conference in Tehran that Iran would continue to answer any military action by the United States or other countries. Asked whether the latest attacks marked a change of course as talks with Washington have stalled, he replied that Tehran was acting in its own security interests and would not be held back by others.

Separately, the Iran-backed Houthis are increasing pressure on government positions around Aden, Yemen’s interim capital. Saudi-backed government forces said they had pulled back from their Bab el-Mandeb offensive in order to concentrate on defending Aden.
items.cav: The sources do not say whether the drones caused any damage, and the tanker sinking is a Revolutionary Guards claim that has not been independently verified. One part of the reporting mentions a strike on Tehran, but the rest of the account describes strikes on Bahrain and Iranian coastal and naval sites, so the details of that strike are unclear.
items.op: Condemning an attack on a neighbouring state is right, but the principle of international law must apply to every side. US strikes on Iranian sites and Iranian claims about mines both need scrutiny. Claims that shape the war, including the tanker sinking, should be verified independently before they are repeated as fact.

items.t: ASEAN offers Myanmar’s sidelined leaders a phased route back to summits, tied to peace-plan progress
items.s: Southeast Asian leaders have agreed to re-engage Myanmar’s government step by step, but a full return to high-level meetings hinges on advances in a regional peace plan. Fighting continues across the country.
p: Myanmar still belongs to the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, yet its political figures have been kept out of summits and foreign ministers’ gatherings since 2021, when the army took power and removed the elected administration headed by Aung San Suu Kyi. The takeover set off a civil war that has not ended.

According to a joint statement issued by the leaders, the bloc could slowly restore Myanmar’s complete political representation if it shows lasting and tangible headway on its five-point peace plan. The approach is designed to move in stages and to respond to what is happening inside the country.

Critics of the plan note that it has produced few results since it was adopted, and clashes persist between the military and pro-democracy and ethnic armed groups. Thailand has argued for closer contact since Min Aung Hlaing assumed a civilian presidency this year, after a vote that monitors rejected as a sham.

Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. put the question directly at the leaders’ retreat in Manila, asking what more the group could offer Myanmar. He called for workable steps to move the peace plan forward and to back a process that is inclusive and led by Myanmar itself.

The agenda also covers trade, regional security and coordinated fuel supply arrangements, as the war in Iran has disrupted energy flows. Separately, Australia and the Philippines signed a defence pact on Sunday, and Canada and the Philippines said on Saturday they had wrapped up free trade talks.

A draft code of conduct for the South China Sea is still unfinished. Philippine Foreign Secretary Theresa Lazaro put the ASEAN–China negotiations at 80% complete, though diplomats told AFP that a deal was unlikely in Manila. Chinese Premier Li Qiang is representing Beijing at the gathering.

US President Donald Trump is expected to join late in the summit on Tuesday and hold meetings with leaders of India, Japan and Australia, the other Quad members. Activists plan to protest that day, partly over a US-backed industrial project north of Manila that they say could push Indigenous families from their land. The Philippines will pass the rotating ASEAN chair to Singapore next year, with Thailand due in 2028.
items.cav: The sources do not define what counts as progress on the peace plan or set a timeline for restoring Myanmar’s representation. Trump’s planned meetings are reported as expectations, not confirmed outcomes. The 80% figure comes from the Philippine foreign secretary, while diplomats doubted a deal was near.
items.op: Tying Myanmar’s return to a peace plan that has delivered little since 2021 risks turning engagement into a holding pattern. Staged re-entry can be pragmatic, but it must come with measurable benchmarks and public reporting. Otherwise ASEAN rewards the coup leadership without any accountable result.

items.t: US pitch would tie Ukraine’s NATO membership to giving up Donbas, Zelenskyy says
items.s: Washington has reportedly proposed a route into NATO for Ukraine on condition that Kyiv cede the Donbas region, a demand Russia has made as a condition for ending the war. Kyiv has not accepted the idea.
p: The United States has floated a new pathway for Ukraine to join the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, an aspiration Kyiv has pursued since applying in September 2022, roughly a few months after Russia’s full-scale invasion. According to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the proposal would require Ukraine to give up the whole of the Donbas region in the east.

Zelenskyy said the idea was conveyed to him by Trump’s negotiators, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, during the latest US-mediated talks between Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates. The two envoys then met Vladimir Putin in Moscow, before briefing Zelenskyy in Dublin ahead of a meeting of European leaders there. The account of the offer comes from Zelenskyy; the sources reviewed do not include a direct public statement from the US envoys.

Zelenskyy told reporters that the Americans had asked whether Ukraine would withdraw from Donbas if it joined NATO. He described the question as part of an “extremely difficult” conversation that would shape European security, and said that NATO was “back on the agenda”. He also said the idea of trading territory for NATO membership had not previously been raised by alliance members.

Kyiv’s position, as restated by Zelenskyy, is that it will not give up any of its territory. He said that if a deal included security guarantees, the right to keep a strong, well-funded army and funds to rebuild the country, he would hold a national referendum on ceding territory in exchange for NATO membership. Russia’s stance is that Ukrainian membership would bring a “harsh response”, and Putin has demanded that NATO pull back forces from countries bordering Russia.

Analysts quoted by Al Jazeera were sceptical. Ian Lesser of the German Marshall Fund said the proposal, if accurate, clearly reflects a long-held view in US administration circles that Ukraine should make territorial concessions. He added that it was hard to imagine Moscow agreeing to the NATO element, and that some alliance members would also be doubtful. Chris Featherstone of the University of York called the idea a major departure from earlier US positions, given Trump’s repeated criticism of NATO and his public dispute with Zelenskyy, and questioned whether Trump could bring other allies on board.

NATO members remain divided on offering Ukraine membership during an ongoing war, although most agree on strong support for Kyiv. Featherstone suggested the proposal may be an attempt to test Ukraine’s refusal to cede land, rather than a settled plan. Whether the offer is genuine, and whether any of the parties would accept it, remains unclear from the reporting available.
items.cav: The core claim about the US offer rests mainly on Zelenskyy’s account of private talks; the envoys’ own words are not quoted in the sources. Analysts describe the proposal as possibly inaccurate or a test, and no sources confirm the Kremlin’s response to the NATO element.
items.op: A peace settlement that trades a sovereign nation’s territory for its own security guarantees would reward the invader and undermine the principle that borders cannot be redrawn by force. Any deal touching Donbas should be made in public, with its terms open to scrutiny by Ukrainians and by NATO’s members, not negotiated behind closed doors.

items.t: SpaceX catches upper part of Starship rocket on return to Earth in first-ever attempt
items.s: SpaceX caught the upper part of its Starship rocket between mechanical arms as it returned to Earth on Saturday, a first for a spaceship, according to reports from Euronews and the BBC. The same launch also saw the booster fail to return to the launch site.
p: According to Euronews, the upper section came back to Earth on Saturday and was caught between two mechanical “chopstick” arms at Starbase in Texas. The BBC reported the same achievement and said the arms are nicknamed chopsticks.

Starship lifted off from Starbase on Friday and orbited Earth 14 times, deploying 26 satellites for Elon Musk’s Starlink internet constellation, Euronews reported. After a journey of about 22 hours, the craft approached Texas’ east coast, and its three Raptor engines ignited as it descended toward the launchpad.

SpaceX celebrated the result on social media. Musk wrote on X that he had “hugged ship 42” upon its return. Crowds at the site cheered as the arms closed around the spacecraft for the first time, a moment the company said “changed everything.”

The BBC said the ship returned at around 15:20 local time, a few minutes behind schedule. Euronews noted that spaceships had previously been single-use vehicles, which made each launch particularly expensive. Starship is also lined up to serve as a landing system for NASA’s Artemis Moon landing mission.

The day was not a clean sweep. SpaceX had hoped to catch both the booster and the upper stage. The booster’s catch was aborted minutes after launch. SpaceX said its guidance system triggered an automated abort and the booster diverted to an offshore landing, and that the boostback burn ended early due to low fuel mass. The company said the root cause was under investigation. The BBC described the booster as diverted to the ocean and bursting into flames just above the sea.
items.cav: The two outlets describe the booster’s fate differently: Euronews reports an offshore splashdown in the Gulf, while the BBC says it burst into flames just above the sea. The cause of the booster fault is still under investigation, and the sources do not explain it. The praise from SpaceX and Musk is company and personal commentary, not independent verification.
items.op: A catch of a returning spacecraft is a real engineering milestone, but celebration should not replace scrutiny. SpaceX should publish a full analysis of the booster failure, including its timeline and fuel data, so outside observers can judge what went wrong. Transparency, not spectacle, is what turns a test flight into lasting progress.

items.t: Copper wire upgrade behind US flight shutdown, transport secretary says
items.s: A nationwide US ground stop that disrupted thousands of flights was caused by a technical problem during a copper wire upgrade, Transport Secretary Sean Duffy has said. The government is still trying to establish the root cause.
p: Air traffic controllers suspended take-offs across the United States for four hours on Friday, a move that led to thousands of cancellations and widespread travel disruption. Duffy told a news conference that the problem followed work to upgrade the system.

Duffy said the government was trying to determine whether the failure resulted from “incompetence” by the company carrying out the upgrades or from faulty equipment. Officials, including Duffy, had earlier blamed outdated equipment.

According to Duffy, a contractor, the technology provider L3Harris, was switching air traffic control systems from copper wire to fibre-optic cable. He described the US telecommunications system as very old, saying the type of wire involved was being discontinued.

Duffy explained that a router being worked on had begun flooding other air traffic control systems and caused communication problems with aircraft. Authorities then halted take-offs on safety grounds. The government is now examining whether the wire replacement or the router fault was the root cause.

The ground stop was lifted on Friday evening, but its effects carried into Saturday as airlines worked to clear a backlog. Flight tracking data cited by the BBC suggested more than 15,000 US flights were delayed or cancelled on Friday, affecting an estimated 1.5 million passengers. On Saturday, more than 5,900 flights were cancelled and 7,000 delayed. Some flights from the UK and Europe were also cancelled. The Federal Aviation Administration said the schedule should return to normal by the end of Sunday.

US officials said they did not believe a cyber-attack was responsible. FAA head Bryan Bedford said there was “zero evidence” of anything nefarious, though Duffy said the investigation into the exact cause was still under way. L3Harris said it had completed more than 70% of its assigned modernisation work before the shutdown and was supporting the FAA’s inquiry.

Duffy warned that a similar failure could happen again unless Congress approves upgrades to air traffic control infrastructure. President Donald Trump has requested $30.1bn for those upgrades, and Republicans control both chambers of Congress.
items.cav: The cause is not yet established: the sources report that the government is still weighing the wire replacement against a router fault, and that the contractor’s role has not been confirmed by any finding. Disruption figures come from flight tracking data and an estimate of passenger numbers, not an official tally. The FAA’s view that no cyber-attack was involved is reported as an official position, and the investigation’s conclusions have not been published.
items.op: Four hours of grounded flights should prompt more than reassurance. The public deserves a clear, published account of whether a contractor’s work, ageing equipment or both caused the failure, and of what Congress will fund. Safety systems demand transparency, and officials who promise upgrades should be held to them.

items.t: US judge temporarily blocks Trump’s plan to overhaul historic Washington golf course
items.s: A federal judge has temporarily halted a plan to close and redevelop a historic public golf course in Washington, another setback for President Donald Trump’s effort to turn it into a championship-level course.
p: Judge Ana Reyes issued a 30-page decision on Saturday that pauses the federal government’s plan to shut East Potomac Park, which was due to close from 15 November for renovations. The park lies near the Jefferson Memorial, about two miles south of the White House.

Trump announced in October that the course would be rebuilt over 15 months into a facility that is open to the public yet designed to a very high standard and able to host major tournaments. He has described the existing layout as worn out, with dangerous trees and a failing seawall.

Reyes found that the administration’s explanations for the closure were “pretextual,” and concluded that officials had breached at least two federal laws “to meet an arbitrary deadline.” In her words, the government was seeking to shut a historic park that residents across the city use every day, with no end date.

The order keeps the park open, but it does not require the administration to keep golf running there. Reyes did add, however, that officials may not treat the lack of golf as grounds for barring visitors.

The DC Preservation League brought the case, arguing that the redevelopment breaks federal rules and statutes. Earlier, Reyes stopped the National Park Service from felling trees or making permanent changes without advance warning, after hundreds of trees had come down on short notice. Democracy Forward, which represents the group, welcomed the latest ruling.

The litigation has also grown acrimonious. Reyes has opened an ethics inquiry into whether government lawyers repeatedly misled her about the closure timeline, while the Justice Department has accused her of exceeding her authority and has asked her to step aside. She refused. The Interior Department, Justice Department and White House did not immediately reply to requests for comment.

At present the park offers three golf courses with 36 holes in total, a miniature golf course and a paved loop frequented by cyclists and runners. The plan would replace all of that with one 18-hole championship layout, which Trump has suggested could stage events such as the US Open and the Ryder Cup.
items.cav: The sources differ on timing: an NPR summary describes a two-week delay, while the Guardian and BBC reports do not give a duration for the block. The reporting also relies on the judge’s written decision as quoted by outlets, and the White House had not responded at the time of publication.
items.op: Courts are doing what the public should expect when a government moves quickly and skips notice: it must justify itself on the record. Transparency about why a public park is closed matters more than who wins the golf course. The pointed question is why the administration rushed past its own legal duties.

items.t: Zelenskyy says US asked whether Ukraine would leave Donbas for Nato membership
items.s: Kyiv’s president says Washington has asked whether Ukraine would give up part of the Donbas in return for joining Nato. He says he will not hand over territory, but would take a deal to a referendum if security guarantees and funding came with it.
p: In remarks to reporters, released by his office on Saturday, Zelenskyy said US officials had for the first time put a question to Kyiv: would Ukraine pull back from areas of the eastern Donbas that Russian forces do not hold, if it were admitted to Nato? He said the query showed that the alliance was back on the table.

He warned that such an arrangement, which could form part of a wider postwar security order for Europe, might let Moscow weaken Nato and redraw frontiers. In his view, steps of that kind tend to bring about wars or escalation. The report does not explain how the American side framed the idea.

Zelenskyy held that Ukraine is not prepared to cede land. However, he said he would let voters decide in a national referendum if the country were offered a full package: security guarantees, a robust and well-financed army, and money to rebuild. He also ruled out neutrality, which he said would require changing the constitution, and noted that Ukraine is not in Nato at present.

He pushed back on Moscow’s demand that a broad European security agreement come first, before the terms for ending the fighting are set. His stance echoed that of European leaders who met in Dublin on Friday. In his words, the war has to end before anything else is reshaped.

Jared Kushner, the envoy and son-in-law of US President Donald Trump, said on Saturday that Washington is working to bring Russia and European governments into direct talks. That followed trilateral meetings among the US, Russia and Ukraine earlier in the week, which reportedly produced an agreement that European countries will take part in future negotiations. Neither Washington nor Nato had publicly responded to the Donbas-for-membership idea.

Separately, Zelenskyy accused SpaceX of being untruthful about limits on Ukraine’s Starshield satellite system. He called the speed restrictions, in place for five days, political rather than technical. Ukrainian drones, he said, can no longer intercept incoming jet-powered Shahed drones. Kyiv suspects the slowdown is a deliberate US move to press him into concessions to Putin, and the report includes no reply from SpaceX.

Macron posted on social media that those seeking to cut aid to Ukraine are effectively trying to impose an unjust peace on Kyiv and, by extension, on Europe, which he described as a path to another war. Elsewhere, Russia’s defence ministry, quoted by the RIA news agency, said it had hit a cargo ship at the Ukrainian port of Chornomorsk that was supplying the Ukrainian military. Ukraine’s General Staff said its strikes set oil storage tanks ablaze at the Samara pipeline station, a key node in Russia’s oil export network, and Ukraine’s Emergency Service reported 22 people injured in a Russian attack on Zaporizhzhia.
items.cav: The account of the US question comes solely from Zelenskyy, and Washington and Nato had not commented, so the American position remains unconfirmed. The Russian claim about the cargo vessel and the SpaceX allegations are also one-sided, and the report does not give the other sides’ full responses.
items.op: Any deal trading Ukrainian land for a security promise should be made in the open, with affected people given a say. Zelenskyy’s referendum offer is the right instinct, but it means something only if the terms are public and the process honest. Quiet bargaining over borders risks the same war under a new name.

items.t: Italy fines Meta €805m over Android users’ photo access without specific consent
items.s: Italy’s data protection authority has fined Meta €805m, or about $887m, for accessing photos and videos on Android devices through the Facebook app without specific consent. Meta says it will appeal.
p: Italy’s data protection authority has fined Meta €805m (about $887m) for accessing photos and videos from Android users without their specific consent. The regulator said the Facebook app gave Meta access to images, videos and related metadata belonging to Italian users, and that people were not properly informed about this.

According to the authority, roughly 20 million smartphone users in Italy were affected. The regulator said they were not made aware that the app could reach their photo galleries, a point it linked to a single app-wide authorisation that came after a notice asking users to enable other features.

The case concerns a feature, available since 2023, that suggests photos and videos from a user’s phone gallery as ideas for posts while they browse. The regulator said that Facebook’s notice did not make clear that the permission would also allow those suggestions to be generated.

In setting the size of the penalty, the authority said it weighed the large number of people affected and the length of the breach, which it said was still continuing for users who had not updated the app or who had already agreed to the system. It also cited what it called Meta’s lack of cooperation during the investigation.

The regulator has ordered Meta to change how the feature works. According to the BBC, the company has 60 days to disable it by default and to seek users’ consent through a separate request. Under the requirements described, Meta must also clearly explain what the feature does and how to switch it off.

Meta responded that it “strongly disagree[s]” with the regulator’s assessment and with the level of the fine. In a statement given to the BBC, the company said the feature helps people post photos and videos and that users must grant permission on their device before it can operate.

The Guardian reported that the fine is roughly 0.4% of the group’s annual turnover, which it put at $201bn in 2025. It also reported that the penalty is among the largest an Italian authority has imposed on a technology company, below a 2021 fine of more than €1.1bn against Amazon for breaching competition law.

Both outlets also referred to a separate case in the United States. The BBC said a judge in New Mexico ordered Meta to pay $25bn after finding that the company had misled the public about how it handled user data. The Guardian described the order as coming from authorities in New Mexico, a difference in wording that the sources do not explain.
items.cav: The sources differ on who imposed the New Mexico penalty, with the BBC saying a judge ordered it and the Guardian saying authorities did. Meta’s account of the feature is its own and has not been independently tested, and the reports do not say whether the appeal will suspend the fine.
items.op: Users should not have to discover by accident that an app can reach their private photo library. Meta’s argument that permission exists in device settings misses the point: consent has to be specific and understood, not buried in a bundled prompt. The regulator’s insistence on clear notice and a fresh opt-in is the minimum transparency that large platforms owe their users.

items.t: Official works two NFL games after nationwide FAA halt upends weekend sports travel
items.s: A nationwide Federal Aviation Administration flight halt on Friday forced leagues and clubs across the United States to reshuffle officials and travel plans. Some of the knock-on effects were still visible on Sunday.
p: Don Willard, an NFL official, is set to work two games on Sunday. The FAA’s nationwide halt on Friday, which lasted several hours, put his original plans in doubt. He is due to call the Miami Dolphins against the Indianapolis Colts at 1pm ET, then drive 112 miles east to officiate the Pittsburgh Steelers against the Cincinnati Bengals on Sunday Night Football.
Because NFL teams generally travel the day before a game, the league’s Sunday slate absorbed much of the shock. Still, the stoppage required changes to officiating crews across the league.

The NBA also had to adjust its referee assignments as travel problems lingered into Saturday. Brian Forte took a place in the Chicago-Minnesota crew, succeeding Jason Goldenberg, while Jenna Schroeder moved into the Dallas-Cleveland game in Forte’s spot. In Brooklyn-Memphis, Michael Smith was added to the three-person crew late in the afternoon because another referee could not reach the arena in time. Later on Saturday, Brent Barnaky and CJ Washington were assigned to Denver-New Orleans.

Sport returned gradually to its usual rhythm on Saturday, though clubs were still coping with the aftermath. Many college football sides arrived the day before kickoff, and several fixtures were held back by hours so that visiting squads could get in and prepare. Utah’s trip to Arizona and Arizona State’s trip to Central Florida were both delayed three hours, while Auburn chose charter buses. The one notable exception was Mississippi’s No 19 game at Oklahoma, which was switched to Sunday with a 1pm ET start.

Other sports felt it too. The Southern California women’s basketball squad was taken off its aircraft and spent the night in Los Angeles, setting off for Greenville only on Saturday afternoon. Fairleigh Dickinson learned late on Friday that its flight to Ohio State had been scrapped, and coach Stephanie Gaitley opted for a 10-hour coach journey on Saturday morning rather than an overnight departure. The Kansas City Current told ESPN they were working with the NWSL and their charter operator to reach their Sunday semi-final in New York in time. Most of the 14 NHL fixtures on Saturday were largely untouched, since the majority of clubs had already landed, though the San Jose Sharks did not arrive in Utah until late Friday.

The Cleveland Cavaliers faced the most severe NBA disruption. Unable to fly out of Miami on Friday night, they departed at 8.54am on Saturday to meet the Dallas Mavericks that evening. Donovan Mitchell said he would rather have seen the game moved, but said the squad would “make adjustments” and push on. A reschedule was impractical, given that the Cleveland arena hosts events on 11 straight days. The club listed Mitchell, James Harden, Peyton Watson and Jarrett Allen as questionable, and all four had started Friday’s game in Miami.
items.cav: The sources do not explain what triggered the FAA halt or give more detail than “several hours”. Willard’s Sunday logistics and the Cavaliers’ injury status come from press reporting rather than official league statements, and the Current’s remarks are the club’s own account.
items.op: Leagues absorbed this disruption quietly, but a federal flight halt should not leave fans and players guessing. The FAA and the leagues owe the public a clear account of what went wrong and what contingency plans exist. Without one, the next stoppage will be met with the same improvisation.

items.t: SpaceX’s Starship upper stage returns to launch tower after orbit, though booster is lost
items.s: SpaceX’s Starship returned to its Texas launch tower on Saturday, with the upper stage caught by the tower’s mechanical arms. The booster, however, was lost in the Gulf of Mexico, so the planned double catch did not happen.
p: The craft’s 15th test flight had been designed as a double-catch mission, in which both stages would come back intact to the launch site instead of being recovered from the ocean, as on some earlier flights. That plan fell apart on Friday, when the booster diverted a few minutes after takeoff and exploded over the Gulf of Mexico.

SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot said early on Saturday that the booster had behaved as designed. In his account, it detected that it was not in the position needed to proceed with a catch. SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk added that the booster was “slightly low on fuel”, a reason that comes from Musk alone and that the company’s statement, as reported, does not repeat.

The upper stage, a 171ft (52-metre) vessel, completed a 22-hour mission in which it orbited Earth 14 times before descending into the tower’s arms. The company said this was the first time it had caught an upper stage, which it described as a step towards making the megarocket reusable.

The timing matters for Nasa, which has contracted SpaceX and Jeff Bezos’s Blue Origin to help return astronauts to the lunar surface, with a target date of 2028. Nasa administrator Jared Isaacman praised the flight on X, writing “Making more believers by the day”. Isaacman is an ally of Musk, who advised Donald Trump to appoint him to lead the agency.

Musk said on a recent earnings call that SpaceX plans to increase Starship test flights to once a week, and later to twice a week. Reusability is central to his argument that space travel costs can be cut sharply. He has also promoted a plan to send people to Mars.
The flight also deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites, which supports the growth of Musk’s satellite internet business.
items.cav: The fuel explanation for the booster’s loss comes only from Musk and is not independently confirmed in the available reporting. The evidence also does not say what caused the booster to move off course, or whether the upper stage faced any problems during the flight.
items.op: Public money is flowing into a private company’s rocket programme, and the agency’s leader has close ties to its founder. Nasa should publish the contract terms and its safety findings in full, so that taxpayers can judge whether the lunar plan is working.

items.t: US blames equipment upgrade for longest nationwide FAA ground stop since 9/11
items.s: US officials say maintenance on an aging telecommunications system may have caused an hours-long halt to all domestic air traffic. The cause has not been confirmed, and the airspace stop has left thousands of flights disrupted.
p: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said at a news conference in Washington on Saturday that routine maintenance performed the previous day could be to blame. The work involved upgrading a router from copper to fibre at a remote location. Duffy said “contractor error or a faulty piece of equipment” caused the router to flood other devices in the air traffic control system with connection attempts.

According to Duffy, the system received about 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds. The resulting disruption to radar feeds and communications between controllers and aircraft led to the decision to halt flights nationwide. He said safety was the priority and the airspace was shut down.

The Transportation Department identified the contractor on the work as L3Harris, a US aerospace and defence company tasked with modernising the FAA’s communications system. Duffy said officials were still trying to establish whether the fault lay in installation or in the router itself. “We haven’t determined what the fault was,” he said. He added that the company “didn’t meet the moment”, and said he would hold people accountable once the facts were known. Al Jazeera said it had contacted L3Harris for comment and had not yet received a reply.

Officials also addressed concerns that a cyberattack was responsible. Duffy said the government did not believe that was the case, pointing to systems returning to service once the work at the location was isolated. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said he saw no evidence of anything malicious and attributed the outage to an equipment error. He said a root cause analysis would be made public when it is available.

The stop was the longest nationwide halt since 9/11, according to the FAA, and only the second nationwide stop since then. Bedford said crews and aircraft were out of position for about 12,000 flights that were lost. He expected roughly 4,000 to 5,000 of the 41,000 flights scheduled for Saturday to be cancelled, and said full schedule integrity was expected by the end of Sunday.

A separate summary from a second news outlet reports that the ground stop was lifted and that officials said the disruption was not caused by a cyberattack or a sweeping Microsoft outage. That article’s full text was not available for this report, so its details could not be checked against the wider account.
items.cav: The root cause is still unconfirmed; the explanations so far come from officials, and the contractor has not responded. The Microsoft claim comes only from a short summary by a second outlet, and the outage figures are the FAA’s own estimates.
items.op: Air travellers and the public are owed a clear answer, not early blame. The FAA should publish its root cause analysis in full and say who was responsible for the router before accountability is announced. Officials who promise consequences must show the evidence that justifies them.

items.t: Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins wins Alaska governor’s race, first Democrat in the seat since 1998
items.s: Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins has won Alaska’s governor’s seat, the first Democratic win there in nearly three decades. The result is part of a wider run of Democratic gubernatorial gains after the 3 November midterms.
p: The Associated Press called the race on Friday, about 10 days after the polls closed. Kreiss-Tomkins, a former Alaska state legislator known widely as JKT, defeated three Republican opponents, including a candidate backed by Donald Trump. He becomes the first Democrat elected governor of Alaska since 1998.

Kreiss-Tomkins returned to politics after a comeback campaign, three years after leaving the Alaska house of representatives. He is 37. According to the Guardian, he travelled widely across the state and built support around economic concerns and a promise to change the direction of government.

His platform focused on affordability, full funding for public education and a requirement that all oil and gas producers pay corporate income taxes. He also called for a temporary halt to new datacenter developments until state lawmakers set rules for their construction.

He sharply criticised the outgoing Republican governor, Mike Dunleavy, saying Alaska had become “broken” during his eight years in office. He pointed in particular to the state’s ferry system, which he said had been left in disarray as service to many communities was drastically reduced. The ferries are a key link for south-east Alaska towns without road connections.

“Alaskans are hungry for change,” Kreiss-Tomkins said during the campaign. He has also said he will assemble a cabinet drawn from Democrats, Republicans and independents. Alaska uses ranked-choice voting, but he won more than 50% of first-choice votes, so no further counting rounds were needed.

The Alaska win follows a close Democratic victory in Kansas, where state senator Cindy Holscher defeated Republican state senate president Ty Masterson, who had Trump’s endorsement. Democrats also won governor’s races in Georgia, Iowa, Nevada, Ohio and Texas. The Guardian reports that the party now holds 30 governorships and a majority of governors’ offices for the first time since 2010. In Texas, Gina Hinojosa becomes the state’s first Hispanic governor and the first Democrat elected there in 35 years.

Separately, Alaska Public Media reported that Democrat Mary Peltola was leading Republican incumbent Dan S Sullivan in the US Senate race with few ballots left to count, and MS Now described that race as leaning Democratic. The Guardian attributes the broader Republican setback partly to Trump’s unpopularity, noting that many Republican lawmakers stayed loyal to him even as polls suggested voters did not back his immigration crackdown, tariffs, the war with Iran or his signature domestic policy bill.
items.cav: The Alaska Senate count was still incomplete, so the Peltola lead is reported, not final. Trump’s unpopularity as a cause of the Republican defeat is the Guardian’s characterisation, and the sources do not give the poll figures behind it.
items.op: Election results that take ten days to call remind us how much depends on careful, transparent counting. Voters in Alaska deserve clear public accounts of the ferry cuts and tax promises Kreiss-Tomkins has made, and he should be held to every one of them.

items.t: Zelenskyy says Washington floated ceding Donbas land for NATO membership
items.s: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says American negotiators have raised giving up parts of eastern Donbas as a condition tied to joining NATO. He says he has turned down any transfer of territory.
p: Zelenskyy told reporters that American negotiators had suggested Ukraine could surrender portions of eastern Donbas and, in return, gain a route into NATO. He spoke after the most recent Russia-Ukraine negotiating sessions held in Abu Dhabi and Ireland. His office published the remarks on Saturday.

According to Zelenskyy, this was the first occasion on which anyone had connected NATO membership with territorial concessions. He recounted that US representatives had asked whether Ukraine would leave Donbas if it became a member. The districts they referred to, he said, are areas that Moscow does not currently govern, and he rejected handing them over.

The Ukrainian leader argued that Vladimir Putin's push to alter European frontiers is a established reality, and that he believes it forms part of a wider plan to rewrite security arrangements on the continent. He warned that such steps tend to produce armed conflict or further escalation. Putin has repeatedly treated Ukraine's accession to NATO as an unacceptable line, and has cited that issue among his reasons for the 2022 invasion.

Zelenskyy indicated that he would submit any surrender of Donbas territory to a nationwide vote, but only if Kyiv were offered a broad set of commitments. Those would include protective assurances, military and rebuilding money, and a plan for recovery from Washington and other allies. He also made clear that no deal would treat occupied areas as belonging to Russia. Neutrality, he added, could not be adopted without amending the constitution.

The diplomatic effort has unfolded alongside heavy fire. Russian officials said on Friday that roughly 1,200 Ukrainian drones had been launched toward Russian territory, with energy facilities among the intended targets. Ukrainian authorities, for their part, reported strikes on a hospital and on the port city of Odesa.

At the Irish summit, EU leaders resolved that any European delegation to future Ukraine talks should be made up of five large military states, namely Britain, which is outside the EU, together with France, Germany, Italy and Poland, plus EU officials. That group would negotiate with American and Ukrainian counterparts, but would not sit down with Russia.
items.cav: The US proposal is reported only through Zelenskyy’s account, and the evidence contains no US comment or Russian response. The drone figure comes from Russian officials, and the hospital and port attacks are reported by Ukraine alone.
items.op: Territory should not be traded through private proposals that the public hears about only later. If Kyiv is to weigh ceding land, the terms, the American commitments and the referendum must be made public and tested openly. Any deal that rewards an invasion by redrawing borders would set a dangerous precedent for Europe.

items.t: Trump, Putin and Xi to hold trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, White House says
items.s: The White House says Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping plan to meet next week in China, on the fringes of an Asia-Pacific summit. Nuclear arms reduction is expected to feature, though Beijing has not formally responded.
p: Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are planning a meeting in Shenzhen, in southern China, according to the White House. Spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters the talks would be historic. The meeting would take place while Trump is attending the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.

Wales said Trump intends to raise the “reduction of nuclear weapons” during the discussions, arguing that their spread is dangerous. US officials cited by AFP said Iran may also come up, but Ukraine will not. A senior US official told news agencies that no agreement was expected from the talks.

Russia has confirmed the meeting. Chinese state media, citing a foreign ministry spokesman, reported that Xi would hold bilateral talks on the APEC sidelines, but they have not mentioned a three-way meeting. Foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said Beijing looked forward to “more practical results” with its partners in trade, connectivity and the digital economy.

The timing is significant. A nuclear weapons control treaty between Washington and Moscow lapsed in February, leaving the largest arsenals without major limits. The United Nations has urged both sides to agree a replacement framework quickly. Trump has suggested a better deal could be struck that includes China, which has been expanding its arsenal.

Trump is set to leave Washington for the Philippines, where he will attend a summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations on Tuesday, before continuing to Shenzhen. The APEC leaders’ gathering runs from 18 to 19 November and brings together 21 member economies. Tesla and SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk is due to accompany Trump to China but will not attend the meeting with Xi and Putin, officials said.

Trump and Xi have tried to signal warmer relations this year, yet little real progress appears to have been made on trade or Taiwan. The war in Iran remains a sticking point, given that Beijing is the largest buyer of Tehran’s oil. Moscow has also leaned heavily on China as a trading partner since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Earlier this month, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov cited “signals confirming readiness” for such talks.
Several points remain unconfirmed. The trilateral format rests on White House statements, Beijing has not publicly endorsed it, and the full agenda beyond nuclear arms has been only partly described.
items.cav: The trilateral meeting rests mainly on White House statements and comments from US officials; China has not confirmed it, and Chinese state media has mentioned only bilateral talks. Whether Iran will be discussed is reported as understood rather than confirmed.
items.op: A leaders’ meeting on nuclear weapons is worth having, but a photo opportunity cannot replace the treaty that lapsed in February. The public deserves a clear agenda, a published account of any outcomes and a timetable for a binding framework. Without transparency, this summit risks becoming another round of warm words.

items.t: US Nationwide Ground Stop Lifted After Longest Since the 2001 Attacks, Officials Blame Aging Air Traffic System
items.s: The US Federal Aviation Administration has lifted a nationwide ground stop that lasted more than four hours, the longest such halt since the 11 September 2001 attacks. Officials say the disruption was not caused by a cyber-attack.
p: The FAA described the Friday stoppage as resulting from “extraordinary circumstances” tied to a communication issue that affected all air traffic control centres. Its first announcement, issued in the afternoon Eastern time, said all departures within the United States would be halted until further notice.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication of a cyber-attack and that everyone was safe. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed the failure on equipment, calling the system “incredibly old” during a news conference on Friday night.

According to FlightAware, more than 8,500 flights were delayed and nearly 8,000 were cancelled on Friday. At the time the order took effect, more than 3,500 aircraft were in the air. Some were diverted to other airports, while others continued to their destinations.

Some flights were later allowed to depart from San Francisco International Airport. Duffy warned that the effects would ripple for several days and said tens of thousands of travellers had been stranded at airports across the country, many without arrangements for the night.

American Airlines said it was concentrating on operating as many remaining flights as possible that evening, and JetBlue said it would resume service on Saturday morning. British Airways advised passengers with US-bound flights to check their status but to go to the airport as planned.

Abroad, Sydney Airport had grounded US-bound flights, although scheduled departures were then expected to leave as planned. Passengers from the UK were warned of possible disruption on Saturday morning. Several flights from London Heathrow to the US were cancelled or delayed, while Manchester said no significant disruption was expected and Gatwick operated normally.

Passenger rights are uneven. Under the FAA Reauthorisation Act of 2024, cancelled or significantly delayed domestic flights, defined as those delayed three hours or more, and international flights delayed six hours or more, must be offered alternative travel or a full refund. Refunds for credit card purchases are due within seven business days, and within 20 days for other payment methods. Airlines in the US are not required to provide meals or accommodation, though some offer support voluntarily. UK law obliges airlines to look after passengers during delays, and the Civil Aviation Authority advises keeping receipts.
Officials’ early explanation is that new equipment added to a decades-old air traffic control system overloaded it.
items.cav: The cause is still preliminary and rests on officials’ statements; the sources do not provide technical details or independent verification. Sources differ on the scale of disruption abroad, and the reported flight figures come from FlightAware rather than the FAA.
items.op: A failure this wide exposes how much national infrastructure depends on systems that were never modernised properly. Officials should publish a full technical account, and passengers deserve clear, enforceable refund rights that do not depend on who is to blame.

items.t: SpaceX Starship booster misses mid-air catch, ship to attempt return
items.s: SpaceX’s Starship booster was diverted to the ocean after a planned catch was aborted, while the upper stage prepared for its own return and a possible catch. The company has yet to decide whether to try grabbing the ship.
p: SpaceX said it would decide later whether to try to catch the upper part of its Starship rocket as it returns to Earth. The company had hoped to catch both the bottom and upper stages using mechanical arms on its launch tower, which it nicknames chopsticks.

The first catch attempt failed. The rocket blasted off from the Starbase site in Boca Chica, Texas, on Friday, and a catch of the Super Heavy booster was planned about six and a half minutes later. Mission control initially gave a “go” for the catch at the tower, but the booster activated an automated abort. It diverted to the ocean, hovered briefly above the water and then exploded, according to the BBC.

The upper section, known as the Ship, continued to space and deployed 26 satellites that form part of the Starlink internet constellation. It is due to complete 14 orbits and return to the launch tower about 22.5 hours after take-off, with a return expected at about 15:15 local time on Saturday.

A SpaceX spokesperson said during a livestream that safety remained the top priority, as the company was still testing manoeuvres it had not attempted before on these vehicles.
